(CNN) -- Christine Beatty, chief of staff for former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty Monday to charges stemming from their text-messaging sex scandal case and will serve four months in jail, according to the Wayne County prosecutor's office. Under a plea deal, Christine Beatty, shown in August at an arraignment in Detroit, will serve five years probation. Beatty pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice, according to Maria Miller, the prosecutor's spokeswoman. Charges of perjury and misconduct against Beatty will be dropped as part of the plea arrangement, she said. Beatty agreed to a plea arrangement under which she will serve five years probation -- the first 120 days to be served in jail -- and pay a $100,000 fine, "based on [Beatty's] ability to pay," Miller said. Beatty will begin serving her jail sentence on January 5, when she will be formally sentenced, Miller said. Kym L. Worthy, prosecuting attorney for Wayne County, released a statement saying she is "very pleased that this defendant admitted her guilt." "We live in an age where greed and protecting one's secrets is glorified and accepted," Worthy said. "Now the city of Detroit, the region and the state of Michigan can truly begin to move forward when this ugly chapter in Detroit's history is put to rest." In September, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor and pleaded guilty to two felony obstruction of justice charges stemming from his efforts to cover up his relationship with Beatty. Like Beatty, Kilpatrick was sentenced to five years probation with the first four months to be served in jail. He is serving that sentence in the Wayne County jail. At the time of his sentencing in October, the judge in the case called Kilpatrick "arrogant and defiant," particularly for a televised speech that aired hours after Kilpatrick entered his pleas. "That night, the community expected to hear a message of humility, remorse and apology," Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner said at Kilpatrick's sentencing. "Instead, we heard an arrogant and defiant man who accused the governor, among others, for his downfall." In addition to his jail and probation sentence, Kilpatrick must also pay the city of Detroit $1 million in restitution, and forfeit any future pension. Initially, Kilpatrick was accused of blocking a criminal investigation into his office and firing a police deputy to cover up an affair with Beatty, then his chief of staff. When that deputy, Gary Brown, filed a whistle-blower suit, Kilpatrick and Beatty denied under oath that an affair had taken place between them. Text messages that contradicted Kilpatrick's and Beatty's denials of an affair were made public in January by the Detroit Free Press, and county prosecutor Worthy charged Kilpatrick and Beatty with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and misconduct in office. The most serious charges would have carried a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison upon conviction. Beatty resigned her post after the text messages were made public. Kilpatrick initially refused to resign after the scandal broke, and Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm called a hearing on whether she should remove him from office at the request of the Detroit City Council. Granholm adjourned those hearings after Kilpatrick pleaded guilty and resigned in September.

**Ex-Detroit official Christine Beatty sentenced to 120 days in jail over text scandal**

**DETROIT (CNN)** — Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff and top aide to former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, was sentenced Monday to 120 days in jail after pleading guilty to obstruction of justice in connection with a text-messaging scandal that rocked the city's leadership.

Wayne County Circuit Court Judge Patricia Fresard sentenced Beatty following a plea agreement reached in December. In addition to her jail term, Beatty was sentenced to five years of probation and ordered to pay $100,000 in restitution to the city of Detroit.

Beatty, 38, choked back tears as she addressed the court and the residents of Detroit before her sentence was handed down.

"I stand before you today knowing that I made a terrible mistake," Beatty said. "I am truly sorry for the pain, embarrassment, and disappointment I have caused to the people of Detroit, the court, and my family."

### A Scandal Born from Text Messages

The high-profile fall of Beatty and Kilpatrick stems from a 2007 civil trial involving a lawsuit filed by former Detroit police officers who claimed they were wrongfully fired for investigating wrongdoing within the mayor’s administration and security detail. 

During that trial, both Beatty and Kilpatrick testified under oath that they were not romantically involved and denied that Beatty played a role in the firing of Deputy Police Chief Gary Brown. 

However, in January 2008, the *Detroit Free Press* published excerpts from thousands of text messages sent from Beatty’s city-issued SkyTel pager. The messages revealed not only an explicit, intimate relationship between Beatty and the married mayor, but also demonstrated that the pair actively conspired to fire Brown and lied about it to conceal their affair.

In one notable exchange from 2003, Beatty texted Kilpatrick: *"I'm tired of lying to protect you."* 

The revelation of the text messages led to criminal perjury and obstruction of justice charges against both Beatty and Kilpatrick in March 2008, paralyzing city politics for months as the duo initially vowed to fight the charges.

### The Downfall of Detroit’s Power Duo

The sentencing marks a final chapter in the legal saga surrounding Beatty, who was once considered one of the most powerful women in Detroit politics. 

Kilpatrick, who was once dubbed the "hip-hop mayor" and viewed as a rising star in the national Democratic Party, was forced to resign in September 2008. He served a similar 120-day jail sentence after pleading guilty to two felony counts of obstructing justice.

Prosecutors noted that Beatty's plea deal avoided a lengthy and costly public trial, though her sentence mirrors the punishment handed down to Kilpatrick.

"Public officials must be held accountable when they violate the trust of the people," Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy said following the hearing. "Lying under oath is a crime, regardless of your title or position."

Beatty was ordered to report to the Wayne County Jail on January 5 to begin serving her sentence.

Here is a detailed chronological summary of what happened to Christine Beatty following the revelation of the text message scandal involving former Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick.

---

### **Background: The Scandal (January 2008)**
In January 2008, the *Detroit Free Press* published thousands of text messages from Christine Beatty’s city-issued SkyTel pager. The text messages proved two major things:
1. Beatty (then Chief of Staff to Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick) and Kilpatrick were engaged in a romantic, extramarital affair.
2. Both had lied under oath during a 2007 civil whistleblower lawsuit brought by former Detroit police officers, who alleged they were fired for investigating the mayor's wrongdoing.

---

### **1. Resignation and Criminal Indictment (2008)**
* **Resignation:** Within days of the *Detroit Free Press* report, Beatty resigned from her position as Chief of Staff in late January 2008. 
* **Criminal Charges:** In March 2008, Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy filed a 12-count felony indictment against Beatty and Kilpatrick. Beatty was charged with perjury, obstruction of justice, and misconduct in office.

---

### **2. Plea Deal and Sentencing (2008–2009)**
* **Guilty Plea:** In December 2008, avoiding a high-profile trial, Beatty entered a plea agreement. She pleaded guilty to two felony counts of misconduct in office for lying under oath about the affair and the firing of Police Deputy Chief Gary Brown.
* **The Sentence:** In January 2009, Wayne County Circuit Judge David Groner sentenced Beatty to:
  * **120 days** in the Wayne County Jail.
  * **Five years** of probation.
  * **$100,000** in restitution to the City of Detroit.
* **Serving Time:** Beatty reported to jail in January 2009 and served 69 days of her 120-day sentence, receiving early release in April 2009 due to good behavior.

---

### **3. Financial Struggles and Bankruptcy (2012)**
Following her release from jail, Beatty faced severe financial hardship due to her criminal conviction, legal fees, and inability to find steady employment in Michigan.
* In 2012, she filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy, listing over $300,000 in debt, which included unpaid legal bills and her court-ordered restitution to Detroit.
* Her legal team worked out payment arrangements allowing her to pay off her restitution over an extended period.

---

### **4. Rebuilding Life: Education and Relocation**
Beatty chose to leave Michigan to start over away from the intense public scrutiny in Detroit.
* **Move to Atlanta:** She relocated to the Atlanta, Georgia area.
* **Higher Education:** She returned to school and earned a Master’s Degree in Social Work (MSW) from Clark Atlanta University.
* **New Career:** Beatty transitioned into non-profit management, community advocacy, and environmental health administration. She worked on initiatives related to lead poisoning prevention and community health equity in Georgia.

---

### **5. Public Reflections and Media Appearances**
Over the years, Beatty has occasionally spoken out about the scandal, focusing on themes of public shaming, redemption, and personal accountability:
* **2012 *Essence* Interview:** Beatty gave her first major sit-down interview, where she expressed deep remorse for her actions, acknowledged the pain caused to the city of Detroit, and discussed the unique public humiliation faced by women involved in political sex scandals compared to male politicians.
* **2014 Centric TV Feature:** She was featured on the show *Being*, detailing her rise in Detroit politics, her downfall, and her journey toward personal healing.
* **Comparison to Kilpatrick:** Unlike Kwame Kilpatrick—who subsequently faced massive federal corruption charges, was sentenced to 28 years in federal prison (later commuted by President Donald Trump in 2021), and initially fought his charges—Beatty largely accepted her local charges, served her time, paid her debts, and maintained a relatively low public profile.

---

### **Where She Is Today**
Christine Beatty continues to live in the Atlanta area, working in social work, behavioral health, and non-profit consultancy. While her name remains inextricably linked to one of the biggest political scandals in Detroit's history, she has largely succeeded in building a quiet, professional post-scandal life centered on community advocacy.

**DETROIT** — Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff and top confidante to ex-Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, pleaded guilty today to two felony counts of obstruction of justice, finalizing a plea deal that brings a dramatic close to the text-messaging scandal that paralyzed Detroit city governance for nearly a year.

Under the terms of the agreement finalized in Wayne County Circuit Court, Beatty, 38, will serve 120 days in the Wayne County Jail, followed by five years of probation. She was also ordered to pay $100,000 in restitution to the City of Detroit. In exchange for her guilty plea, prosecutors dropped perjury and misconduct in office charges that could have carried up to 15 years in prison.

Beatty tearfully admitted in court that she lied under oath during a 2007 civil trial regarding her romantic involvement with Kilpatrick and her role in the firing of a high-ranking police official.

Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy, who led the investigation and brought criminal charges against both Beatty and Kilpatrick, spoke forcefully following the hearing, framing the conviction as a crucial step in restoring integrity to the justice system.

"This case was never about personal relationships, private lives, or political vendettas," Worthy said during a press conference. "It was about the erosion of truth in our courtrooms. When public officials lie under oath, it strikes at the very heart of our judicial system. No one is above the law—not the mayor, and not his chief of staff."

Worthy added that the plea agreement spares the city the expense and strain of a lengthy trial. "Justice was served today," Worthy stated. "Ms. Beatty’s actions led to a massive cover-up that cost Detroit taxpayers millions of dollars. Today, she was finally held accountable."

### The Whistleblower Lawsuit and the Secret Texts

The criminal charges stemmed from a 2007 civil whistleblower trial brought by former Deputy Police Chief Gary Brown and Officer Harold Nelthrope. Brown claimed he was unlawfully fired by Kilpatrick in 2003 because he was investigating allegations of misconduct within the mayor’s executive protection unit, as well as rumors of an unbridled party at the mayor's residence, the Manoogian Mansion.

During the trial, both Beatty and Kilpatrick took the witness stand and swore under oath that they were not romantically involved and that Beatty alone was responsible for Brown’s termination for performance-related reasons. Relying in part on that testimony, a jury awarded $6.5 million to the officers.

To keep the truth hidden, Kilpatrick secretly agreed to settle the lawsuit—along with another related suit—for $8.4 million of taxpayer money on the condition that confidentiality agreements were signed and incriminating evidence remained sealed.

However, in January 2008, the *Detroit Free Press* obtained and published thousands of text messages from Beatty’s city-issued SkyTel pager. The intimate and explicit text messages exposed not only a passionate, long-running affair between Beatty and Kilpatrick, but also revealed that the two actively plotted to fire Gary Brown.

The revelation proved that both officials had committed perjury during the civil trial, triggering a criminal investigation by Prosecutor Worthy's office that resulted in a 12-count indictment against the pair in March 2008.

### Kilpatrick’s Downfall and Resignation

Beatty’s plea follows the fall of Kwame Kilpatrick, once considered a rising star in the national Democratic Party. Dubbed the "Hip-Hop Mayor" when elected at age 31, Kilpatrick saw his political career vanish under the weight of the scandal.

Faced with mounting criminal charges, impeachment proceedings by the Detroit City Council, and a state removal hearing initiated by Governor Jennifer Granholm, Kilpatrick resigned as mayor in September. 

As part of his own plea deal, Kilpatrick pleaded guilty to two counts of obstruction of justice and no contest to assault charges stemming from a separate incident involving a police investigator. He served 120 days in jail, surrendered his law license, was sentenced to four years of probation, and was ordered to pay $1 million in restitution to the city.

With Beatty’s guilty plea, the legal saga surrounding the original text-messaging cover-up reaches its conclusion, leaving the city of Detroit to rebuild public trust in the wake of one of the most contentious political scandals in its history.

Beatty is scheduled to formally begin serving her 120-day jail sentence next month.

* Pay $1 million in restitution to the city.
* Surrender his state law license.
* Serve five years of probation.

Kilpatrick served his jail time late last year and relocated to Texas after his release.

### The Legacy of the Scandal

The scandal paralyzed Detroit’s municipal government for much of 2008, casting a heavy shadow over a city already facing severe economic headwinds. The city ultimately paid out $6.7 million to settle the whistleblower lawsuit that triggered the perjury investigation.

Legal experts noted that while both Beatty and Kilpatrick faced maximum sentences of up to 15 years in prison for the felony obstruction charges, the plea bargains allowed the city to avoid a prolonged, sensational trial.

While today's sentencing closes the chapter on the text-message scandal, both Kilpatrick and Beatty continue to face ongoing scrutiny from federal prosecutors, who are currently conducting a broader corruption investigation into city contracts during Kilpatrick’s tenure. 

Beatty is scheduled to begin serving her 120-day sentence immediately at the Wayne County Jail.

**Byline:** Staff Report  
**DATELINE:** DETROIT — 

Christine Beatty, the former chief of staff and top aide to ex-Detroit Mayor Kwame Kilpatrick, was sentenced to 120 days in the Wayne County Jail today, bringing a formal legal end to a high-profile perjury and cover-up scandal that paralyzed the city’s political leadership for nearly a year.

In exchange for her plea, Wayne County prosecutors dropped more severe charges, including perjury and obstruction of justice, which carried potential sentences of up to 15 years in prison.

Addressing the court in a soft, tearful voice before the sentence was handed down, Beatty offered a direct apology to the residents of Detroit.

"I stand before you today taking full responsibility for my actions," Beatty said. "I apologize to the citizens of Detroit, to the court, and to my family for the pain and disappointment I have caused. I deeply regret my choices."
